# Diagnosing Car Stereo Power Wiring and Memory Retention

The symptoms you are describing—the radio losing presets and shutting down immediately when the ignition is turned off—are classic indicators of incorrect power pinout configuration or a missing constant power source. In automotive electronics, understanding the distinction between "ACC" (Accessory) and "BAT" or "BATT" (Battery/Constant) lines is critical for proper operation.

Based on your voltage readings, the factory harness provides two distinct signals that are often misinterpreted during installation. The wire labeled **Yellow** reads 12V only when the car is running; this is a standard ACC signal. It supplies power to turn on devices like the radio or climate control but disconnects completely when the key is removed. This explains why your unit loses all settings and goes offline once you shut off the engine. The unit interprets the loss of voltage as a command to save state, clear memory, and cut power.

The wire labeled **Red** on the car side shows 12V regardless of whether the ignition is on or off. This indicates it is already wired to a constant battery source (likely fused directly to the chassis battery). Your initial observation that this wire provides constant voltage suggests your installer may have routed it incorrectly, labeling it "ACC" when it should be used as the memory power source.

Your proposed solution of connecting both the Red and Yellow wires on the adapter to the single constant 12V source from the car is functionally correct for keeping memory alive. By tying the ACC input to a constant voltage, you are effectively tricking the head unit into thinking the ignition is always engaged. This prevents it from entering sleep mode or wiping its non-volatile RAM when the actual ignition cycle ends.

However, there is a critical nuance regarding the "bulb" adapter mentioned in your description. Many aftermarket stereos come with a pre-wired accessory cable that includes a small LED indicator bulb on the ACC line. This bulb serves two purposes: it provides feedback to the installer about which wire has power, and it protects the stereo from accidental reverse polarity or short circuits by drawing a minimal current path. If you bypass this specific adapter entirely and hardwire both pins directly to your constant 12V source, ensure that you are not inadvertently creating a ground loop or overloading a fuse meant for intermittent loads.

A safer approach than modifying existing wires is to tap into the Red (constant) line using an additional fuse holder if it isn't already present. You would splice the Yellow wire from your adapter to this tapped constant voltage, while leaving the Red wire connected as usual. This ensures that both the "power on" signal and the "memory retention" signal receive 12V simultaneously.

If you proceed with connecting both wires to the same constant source, verify that the total current draw of your stereo does not exceed the rating of the fuse protecting that specific circuit. Most modern head units consume around 500mA in standby mode; ensuring the fuse is rated for at least 10A or higher on that branch will prevent a blown fuse scenario tomorrow morning.

In professional installations, this constant power line is frequently referred to as the "Memory" wire precisely because it maintains the EEPROM state of the device. Without it, the unit relies solely on the internal capacitor, which drains in seconds once the ACC voltage drops, resulting in the loss of presets and volume settings you observed. Your diagnosis of the wiring labels versus actual voltages was spot-on, and your workaround addresses the root cause effectively, provided current limits are respected.
